messages.body_plain:
Hi DRUG.
I hope this message finds you. I've had a few issues with security down here so have deleted some previous cached d-rug messages of mine off the list-serve as well.

My question is that I am having memory issues in R. I want to merge 2 very large files together based on species name, and keep getting this error message:

"Error: cannot allocate vector of size 1024.0 Mb
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In make.unique(as.character(rows)) :
  Reached total allocation of 16000Mb: see help(memory.size)..."

I've tried reallocating virtual memory space, altering the number of core's accessible by R, removing unnecessary data/ objects, etc.

I know merge is a memory intensive action and wonder if you all know of another, more sensible way to reproduce this. Or, perhaps, some other solution I haven't yet thought of.

Thanks!
Iara

--

messages.body_plain:
Hey y'all,

My best friend is having a baby (boy), and I want to annoy her with lots of name suggestions (especially weird, 19th-century name suggestions ;).  I thought it would be a fun R/dplyr challenge to come up with a function or a bit of code that samples the 'babynames' package for 5 random boys' names from each decade (1880-2020), and send one group of names to her every day (bonus points if I can get R to Tweet them to her, but one step at a time here).

I can do it decade by one decade, manually:

library(babynames)
library(dplyr)
babynamess <- babynames

babynamess %>%
  filter(sex=='M') %>%
  filter(year<=1889) %>%
  sample_n(.,5)

...but I'd like to be able to write a function that pulls 5 names from each decade into a tbl_df.  My first problem is that I can't figure out how to get dplyr to add a 'decades' column, conditional on the year. Does anyone know how to do this?  I'm guessing it's some permutation of (summarize), but I don't know what.

Thanks, hopefully this provides a good little diversion for folks that need one, and I'll be at the drug meeting tomorrow!

Best,
Myfanwy

messages.body_plain:
In dplyr, mutate is used to create new columns or update existing ones, then you’ll want group_by to sample from each decade:
library(babynames)
library(dplyr)
babynamess <- babynames

babynamess %>%
  filter(sex=='M') %>%
  mutate(decade = plyr::round_any(year, accuracy = 10, f = floor)) %>%
  group_by(decade) %>%
  sample_n(.,5)

I’m using the round_any function from the plyr package here because it’s a convenient way to round down to the nearest 10. Many plyr functions interfere with dplyr, though, so I don’t load the whole package but just get the one function with plyr::round_any.

Mazal Tov to your friend!

Noam
​

messages.subject: reassignment within mapply?
messages.body_plain:
Dear D-RUG folks;

Here is a data manipulation task, which I would like to automate, so as to do it within a function. I have a data frame, like this one, in which all the values in each column are identical except the ID variable.
dat <- data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                  V1 = rep(5, 5),
                  V2 = rep(7, 5),
                  V3 = rep(6, 5))

I need to make several different versions of this data frame, each with one column changed to a different value (all values in the column still identical). I have a vector listing the names of the columns to be changed, and a vector listing the new values for each column.
col.names <- c("V1", "V3")
new.values <- c(4, 8)

The final result I am hoping to achieve would be a list of the new versions of the data frame, each with the appropriate column changed to its new value, like this:
new.dat <-
  list(data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                  V1 = rep(4, 5),
                  V2 = rep(7, 5),
                  V3 = rep(6, 5)),
       data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                  V1 = rep(5, 5),
                  V2 = rep(7, 5),
                  V3 = rep(8, 5)))

In attempting to automate this task, here is what I have tried. I created a list of as many copies of the original data frame as there are elements in the vector naming the columns to be changed. Then I attempted to use an mapply statement to reassign the specified columns to their new values. But this did not work as intended.
list.dat <- lapply(col.names, function(x) {dat})

list.dat2 <-
  mapply(function(x, y, z)
           {x[y] <- z},
         list.dat,
         col.names,
         new.values)

I think the problem is that you cannot reassign a column within an mapply statement like that. But I am not sure how to rewrite this to accomplish my objective. Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Bonnie
​

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bonnie,

I think I see a few issues here. First your mapply() needs to return something (not just attempt to modify the dataframe which won't work due to scoping rules) — preferably the modified dataframe. Second, a usual suspect with mappy() is by default the argument SIMPLIFY=TRUE, which almost always makes one's life not simple.

Admittedly I'm not 100% sure what you're doing here, but it seems you want to have (1) a dataframe of changes to be made by row, column, and new value, and (2) apply these changes to the same dataframe storing the different versions in a list. So here's what I'd do:

> dat <- data.frame(ID = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),

+                   V1 = rep(5, 5),
+                   V2 = rep(7, 5),
+                   V3 = rep(6, 5))

> # some fake changes, but kept tidy in a dataframe:
> changes <- data.frame(row=sample(1:nrow(dat), 3), col=sample(2:4, 3), new.value=runif(3))
> changes
  row col new.value
1   3   4 0.9469917
2   2   3 0.4958510
3   1   2 0.3440302
> with(changes, mapply(function(r, c, v) {dat[r, c] <- v; dat}, row, col, new.value, SIMPLIFY=FALSE))
[[1]]
  ID V1 V2        V3
1  1  5  7 6.0000000
2  2  5  7 6.0000000
3  3  5  7 0.9469917
4  4  5  7 6.0000000
5  5  5  7 6.0000000

[[2]]
  ID V1       V2 V3
1  1  5 7.000000  6
2  2  5 0.495851  6
3  3  5 7.000000  6
4  4  5 7.000000  6
5  5  5 7.000000  6

[[3]]
  ID        V1 V2 V3
1  1 0.3440302  7  6
2  2 5.0000000  7  6
3  3 5.0000000  7  6
4  4 5.0000000  7  6
5  5 5.0000000  7  6

Is that what you're looking for?

HTH,
Vince

I think Dave's solution is great — rle() is a nice function. It's worth mentioning Bioconductor actually has an Rle class in S4Vectors (created the same way with the Rle() function) that not only calculates runs, but compresses the vector this way (since runs are common in large genomic datasets). If your data are large, I might recommend this.

Also — point of discussion — +1 if dplyr? In my book that's a -0.5! There's something to be said about using base functions when they're there and lead to solutions as readable as dplyr solutions. Dplyr just creates another library dependency and can lead to some horribly obfuscated code in some cases. Its use of special evaluation also creates really nasty complications if you need to do something programmatically. This isn't to say I don't love dplyr — I really do. But base functions have their place. But in my book readability and simplicity are paramount, and for many tasks base R functions fill this role. </rant> :-)

Vince

messages.body_plain:
Does anyone know of a way of doing full information maximum likelihood (FIML) estimation in R in the context of a mixed effects model?  This method is also sometimes referred to as "direct maximum likelihood" or "raw maximum likelihood".  It is a method that can handle missing data without the need for imputation and is commonly used in structural equation modeling (such as in the R package, lavaan).  But, after much searching, I cannot find an implementation of this method for multilevel modeling in R.  If anyone knows of a way of doing this, please let me know.  Thanks.

Bonnie

messages.subject: Data Carpentry/R workshop Feb 9-10
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

There will be a 2-day workshop on data management and R on Feb 9-10, organized through VetMed.  More details below. This workshop is aimed at those with little to no experience with R.  If you joined D-RUG because you wanted to learn R from scratch, this is an excellent opportunity for getting started.

Michael Levy and I will be amongst the instructors - follow up with us if you have questions.

Noam

------

The Laboratory for Data-Intensive Biology in the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine will be hosting a Data Carpentry workshop on Feb 9-10, 2015.  Registration and a nominal fee ($20) is required for this workshop on a first-come, first-serve basis.  Please read on below for registration instructions.

The workshop will be held in the Shields Library.

Data Carpentry workshops are for any researcher who has data they want to analyze, and no prior computational experience is required. This hands-on workshop teaches basic concepts, skills and tools for working more effectively with data. We will cover data organization in spreadsheets, data cleaning, the command line, and R for data analysis and visualization using examples from biology. Participants should bring their laptops and plan to participate actively. By the end of the workshop learners should be able to more effectively manage and analyze data and be able to apply the tools and approaches directly to their ongoing research.

Data Carpentry's aim is to teach researchers basic concepts, skills, and tools for working with data so that they can get more done in less time, and with less pain.

Preliminary schedule:

* Day 1 morning: Data organization in spreadsheets and data cleaning with OpenRefine
* Day 1 afternoon: Working with data in R
* Day 2 morning: Data analysis and visualization in R
* Day 2 afternoon: Workflows and automating repetitive tasks with command line shell

More information available at:
